sentences.text: This dinosaur is defined by two parallel rows of tall spines running down its neck and back, representing the most extreme elongation of bifurcated neural spines known among dicraeosaurids.
Despite these impressive features, the animal was relatively small for a sauropod, reaching lengths of 9 to 13 meters and weighing approximately 2.5 to 4 metric tons.
It possessed a shorter neck than most other sauropods, consisting of thirteen opisthocoelous cervical vertebrae that formed ball-and-socket joints with neighboring vertebrae.
Like other members of the Diplodocoidea, it had box-shaped snouts and narrow teeth restricted to the front of their jaws.
Its neck and back feature two parallel rows of tall spines that are taller than those of any other known sauropod.

Analysis of growth lines in a rib indicates that the holotype individual of Amargasaurus was at least ten years old, though the absence of an external fundamental system suggests it may not have been fully grown.
The genus Amargasaurus was named by Bonaparte in 1984, and the species was formally described by Salgado and Bonaparte in 1991.
The only known skeleton, specimen MACN-N 15, was discovered in February 1984 by Guillermo Rougier during an expedition led by José Bonaparte.
This virtually complete skeleton, which includes only a fragmentary skull, was found in sedimentary rocks of the La Amarga Formation in the Neuquén Basin.

Based on the orientation of its inner ear and neck vertebrae articulation, the animal probably fed at mid-height, holding its snout at a downward angle of approximately 65 degrees relative to the horizontal.

In a neutral posture, the snout would have rested about 80 centimeters above the ground, while anatomical features suggest the elongated neural spines likely prevented its neck from being raised higher than 270 centimeters.
However, anatomical features also suggest Amargasaurus had increased head mobility, allowing it to graze or uproot vegetation while feeding low to the ground.
Research suggests Amargasaurus had poorer hearing than other studied sauropods because its inner ear lagena was relatively short.

In 1991, Salgado and Bonaparte proposed that Amargasaurus was a slow walker due to its proportionally short forearms and lower legs, but in 1999, Mazzetta and Fariña contradicted this, arguing that the animal was capable of rapid locomotion.
The leg bones of Amargasaurus were sturdier than those of the modern white rhinoceros, an animal adapted for galloping.
Amargasaurus is classified as a member of the family Dicraeosauridae within the order Sauropoda, and it was the first known dicraeosaurid dinosaur from the Cretaceous period.
Amargasaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically from the Barremian to the Aptian stages, between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago.

The exact function and life appearance of Amargasaurus's elongated vertebral spines remain unknown. Salgado and Bonaparte (1991) hypothesized that the spines served as defensive weapons because they tapered toward their tips, while some researchers have proposed that the spines supported two parallel skin sails for display.
